label: Visible signs
rationale: What shows on your body or someone else's: an injury, blood, sweat, a pale or flushed face. These are often followed by daijoubu?
mixUps: An injury takes suru (kega o suru), and blood comes out just like a fever does (chi ga deru, chi deteru yo). Sweat takes kaku (ase o kaku), which is not kaku 'write'. A pale face is kaoiro ga warui (bad colour), while a red face is just kao ga akai.

targets.verbSense: do, make; here it turns the noun kega (injury) into something that happens
targets.trap: Not itaku naru or kizutsuku (mostly hurt feelings): an injury is 'done', kega o suru, even by accident.
targets.use: Heard as kega shita (I got hurt) and as the worried kega nai? (you're not hurt?) after a fall. Name the body part with o and drop kega's own o (ashi o kega shita), or use ni (ashi ni kega o shita); never two o's.

example.ja: サッカーで足怪我しちゃった。
example.english: I hurt my leg playing football.

examplePolite.romaji: sakkaa de ashi o kega shita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: サッカーで足を怪我したんです。
examplePolite.english: I hurt my leg playing football.

targets.verbSense: come out, appear; also leave, go out
targets.trap: 'Bleed' is one verb in English; Japanese says blood comes out, chi ga deru (chi deteru yo). Shukketsu suru is the medical word.
targets.use: Said when you spot a cut: chi deteru yo (you're bleeding), or chi deta (it bled). Ga often drops in casual talk, and when it stops the blood tomaru (chi tomatta?).
targets.notes: A nosebleed has its own word: hanaji ga deru (hanaji deteru yo).

example.romaji: are, yubi kara chi deteru yo.
example.ja: あれ、指から血出てるよ。

examplePolite.romaji: are, yubi kara chi ga dete imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、指から血が出ていますよ。

targets.verbSense: scratch; with sweat or snoring it means to give something off from the body
targets.trap: 'Sweat' is a verb in English, but Japanese uses the noun with kaku: ase o kaku, not ase suru (ase ga deru, 'sweat comes out', is also fine). This kaku is not kaku 'write'.
targets.use: Mostly heard in the past, ase kaita or ase kaichatta (I got all sweaty), after heat or exercise. For dripping with sweat natives say asedaku: asedaku ni natta.
targets.notes: The same kaku goes with embarrassment: haji kaita (I embarrassed myself).

example.ja: 汗かいたから、シャワー浴びたい。
example.english: I'm all sweaty, I want a shower.

examplePolite.romaji: ase o kaita node, shawaa o abite kite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 汗をかいたので、シャワーを浴びてきてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: I got all sweaty. Would it be OK if I had a shower?

targets.trap: Not kao ga shiroi, which sounds like fair skin: 'you look pale' is kaoiro ga warui (kaoiro warui yo). Kao ga aoi also works and sounds stronger; kao ga massao is white as a sheet, from shock, fear or feeling very sick.
partners: guai (condition: guai ga warui = feel unwell)
targets.use: A caring remark to someone who looks ill, kaoiro warui yo, usually followed by daijoubu? Ga often drops, and when they look better it's kaoiro yoku natta ne.
targets.notes: Kaoiro o ukagau (read someone's face) is a separate idiom: checking their mood before you act.

example.english: You look pale. Are you OK?

examplePolite.romaji: kaoiro ga warui desu yo. daijoubu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 顔色が悪いですよ。大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: You look pale. Are you all right?

targets.trap: 'Blush' has no single everyday verb: the face goes red, kao ga akaku naru, or you tereru (get bashful); sekimen suru is bookish.
partners: me (eyes: me ga akai = red eyes)
targets.use: Said to someone flushed from drink, a fever or embarrassment, often teasing: kao akai yo. Ga usually drops; going red as it happens is kao ga akaku naru (kao akaku natteru).
targets.notes: Tereru (get bashful) is the verb behind most blushing: tereteru no?

example.english: Your face is red. Are you drunk?

examplePolite.romaji: kao ga akai desu yo. yotta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 顔が赤いですよ。酔ったんですか？
examplePolite.english: Your face is red. Have you been drinking?

reviewPool.english: make fun of, look down on
embarrass yourself, make a fool of yourself
get some exercise, move your body
be a nice change of pace, do someone good
install an app, get an app
